newsitem.title: USA: Kantor says agency made China obey U.S. export law.
newsitem.headline: Kantor says agency made China obey U.S. export law.

text.p: U.S. Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor on Wednesday defended his department's handling of a $1.6 billion aircraft deal with China in which machine tools may have been improperly diverted to the military.

The New York Times reported on Wednesday that a federal grand jury was investigating whether McDonnell Douglas Corp. or the procurement arm of the Chinese Aviation Ministry knowingly violated U.S. technology export control laws after signing a $5 million side agreement for the sale of machine tools two years ago.

The agreement called for the machine tools to be delivered to a new aviation machinery plant to be built in Beijing. The newspaper reported that the plant was never built and the machinery was diverted to a military factory that produces missiles, violating the terms of the export license.
After the department complained about the violation, China sent the equipment to a joint-venture installation being run with McDonnell Douglas in Shanghai, the newspaper said.

"The Bureau of Export Administration has done a commendable and appropriate job in making sure not only that they're careful in terms of their approval of licenses for dual-use technology but in following up and making sure it's used appropriately," Kantor said at a news conference.

The agency, which is part of the Commerce Department, had approved the export licenses as part of a deal involving the sale of 40 planes, half to be built in California and half in Shanghai, the newspaper said.
"You can't warrant in every case there will never be a situation where some country or some entity doesn't try to take unfair advantage of the situation," Kantor said.
But he added: "I'm not speaking directly to this. I don't think it would be appropriate for me to do so."
In Chicago a McDonnell Douglas Corp. spokesman said the company followed U.S. export law and alerted the government of the diversion after finding out about it in March 1995.
"We're confident that the current investigation will show that McDonnell Douglas violated no laws in the sale of this surplus equipment to the Chinese," corporate spokesman Larry McCracken said.
